**Title:** Same Name, Different Unit: Identifying Source-Specific Units in Web Price Fusion

**Abstract (283 words):**

Web services that fuse prices from many sources assume that the sources quote in one unit. The assumption fails when a source's unit is a claim on the source itself, such as a balance on a platform's ledger, whose value can drift from the unit it is named after. Fusion then reports the drift as a price change, and reliability weights and robust aggregation cannot tell the two apart. A source's unit is never quoted, and any item can move for its own reasons. We model each source's prices as true prices plus a unit offset shared by all its items. Agreement across unrelated items identifies the offset, and a unit anchor, an item whose value is fixed in the true unit, separates a unit shift from demand for the items. We test the approach on cryptocurrency exchanges, whose dollar balances are ledger claims, with public hourly prices from 2017 to 2023. On assets withheld from development, one offset per source-hour removed 85% of the mean-square cross-source price gap, and 30% to 45% in each year from 2020, and its mean correction between two sources that shared a unit was 2.7 bps, against 22.2 bps between two that did not. The anchor, the stablecoin USDT, followed the offset one for one on Binance.US in 2023 (slope 1.00) and carried 71% of it on Bitfinex in 2018 and 2019 (95% interval 56% to 88%), which demand alone would not produce. A monitor built on the offsets raised less than half the false alarms of a plain price-gap rule at equal recall, and in 2023 it separated an exchange's dollar failure from a stablecoin run. Price feeds can state which unit each price is in.

**Suggested keywords:** exchange dollars; unit of account; truth discovery; price feeds and oracles; Web data quality; cryptocurrency markets; reproducibility
